title: Fallthrough Governance & Variant Escrow - Platform Notes
summary: Working notes proposing a lightweight Fallthrough Governor control-plane component that orchestrates regional spillover, tiered capacity pools, and pre-approved model variants ("escrow") for safe, observable graceful degradation.
body:
Context and goal:
We need a concise operational primitive that centralizes short-term decisions when inference capacity or quality is constrained. Existing route-level routing works, but we lack a single control-plane actor that can: 1) absorb cluster-level telemetry, 2) execute temporary policy changes (model substitutions, limited spillover), and 3) provide an auditable, reversible path for degradations.

Proposal (overview):
Introduce a Fallthrough Governor: a transient controlboard (state machine) that listens to regional and global telemetry and emits short-lived policy patches. The Governor’s outputs include per-route model fallthrough chains, region-to-region spillover caps, pool prioritization (hot/warm/cold), and an "escrow release" mechanism to allow pre-approved lower-cost/quality variants to serve when needed.

Key concepts:
- Variant Escrow: a registry of pre-validated alternative models (quantized, trimmed, or different checkpoints) with metadata: quality delta, cost delta, compat notes, and test artifact links. Escrow items are approved by a small cross-functional board and can be auto-enabled by the Governor under configured constraints.
- Tiered capacity: Hot (pinned SLA-backed nodes), Warm (elastic low-latency warm instances), Cold (best-effort, longer start times). Governor reasons about pools and triggers spillover along a preference order.

Inputs the Governor consumes:
- Per-region per-route RPS and token/sec
- Latency percentiles (50/95/99), GPU utilization per pool, batch queue depth
- Error/5xx rates and model-run failure counts
- Reserved vs burst capacity remaining, and KV-cache hit ratios
- Route priority, tenant tier, and recent rollout metadata

Outputs (action types) the Governor can emit:
- Per-route fallthrough: e.g., primary -> slim -> quantized variant with explicit TTL
- Region spillover: allow overflow to specified peer regions with a capped % of traffic
- Pool reprioritization: demote from Hot -> Warm with timeout and rationale
- Escrow release: temporarily permit lower-quality variants for specified routes/tenants
- Admission controls: token throttles, soft-queueing, or reject signals when capacity exhausted

Governor lifecycle and modes:
- Passive: consumes telemetry, only generates advisories and alerts.
- Advisory: suggests policies (console + notifications) but does not enforce.
- Active: thresholds hit -> emits policy changes automatically with conservative defaults and rollback timers.
- Cooldown: metrics stabilized -> staged rollback in safest-first order.
- Manual override: incident commander or platform engineer can force/lock policies via RBAC in Console; every change must be audited.

Escrow selection and pre-qualification checklist (offline):
- Functional smoke tests (per-route prompt-sets) ensuring no catastrophic regression
- Latency and cost profiling on representative infra (hot/warm/cold)
- Quantified quality delta per route (route-specific eval metric or human review if needed)
- Tokenization and KV-cache compatibility or clear fallback mapping
- Licensing and data handling review completed

A simple scoring heuristic (how Governor picks substitutions):
Score = +alpha*(tenant-priority) - beta*(expected-latency) - gamma*(quality-delta) - delta*(cost)
Governor selects highest-scoring variant subject to policy constraints (tenant opt-outs, max simultaneous substitutions). We default to conservative weights favoring quality; product lines may tune weights.

Regional spillover ordering (preferred path):
1) Local warm pool
2) Peer region with low RTT and warm capacity (bounded cap, e.g., 10% per route)
3) Dedicated overflow region (reserved burst nodes)
4) Local escrow variants if cross-region options exhausted
Cross-region decisions include hysteresis and a min-duration window (e.g., 5–10m) to prevent thrash.

Safety and governance guardrails:
- Tenant-level policy: enterprise customers can opt-out of quality-lowering fallbacks; lower tiers can accept more aggressive substitutions.
- Audit trail: every auto or manual action must log: reason, metric snapshot id, actor (auto or username), TTL, and rollback plan.
- Canary scope: automatic policies should first apply to small cohorts (1–5%) and expand on success.
- Rate limits on policy churn: e.g., 1 policy change per route per X minutes to avoid too-frequent toggles.

Operational runbook (short checklist):
Trigger example: 99p latency > 2s for 3 minutes AND GPU queue > 75% for 2 minutes.
Immediate on-call steps:
1) Open Governor UI -> confirm current active policy and TTL.
2) If escrow substitution active: inspect Console sample outputs for representative routes/customers.
3) If outputs unacceptable: escalate to Model-Ops and use manual override to revert; consider immediate cross-region reroute.
4) If Governor inactive and metrics degrading: manually enable local escrow for narrowly targeted high-impact routes.
5) After stabilization: create an incident with governor_policy_id and metric_snapshot_id and tag relevant owner teams.
Post-incident: attach failing prompt-sets and schedule re-eval of escrow items.

Testing and validation plan:
- Synthetic stress tests that saturate GPU queues to validate failover and rollback behavior.
- Chaos tests that kill warm nodes during a spike to exercise spillover decisions.
- Replay recorded traffic to score candidate escrow variants across real traffic shapes.
- Autoscaler integration: ensure Governor changes are rate-limited so they don’t conflict with autoscaler decisions.

Unresolved questions and trade-offs:
- Escrow granularity: per-route vs per-tenant vs model-family; more granularity increases approval overhead.
- Single universal quality metric is hard across heterogeneous routes; need per-route eval harnesses.
- Approval governance: propose a small board (SRE + Model-Ops + Product Owner) to sign escrow items.
- Customer billing/legal: decide whether degraded-quality events require different billing or disclosure.

Concrete next steps (near-term deliverables):
- Draft Governor control API (policy message format + telemetry inputs) — owner: Evan McCarthy — TRACK: PLAT-2028
- Define escrow registry schema and approval UI — owner: Rhea Singh — PR: github.com/redwood/escrow-registry/pull/12
- Run 3 replay tests on low-risk routes and record quality deltas — owner: Anil Rao
- Add audit/logging hooks to Console and incident templates — owner: Nadia Kole

References and artifacts:
- Confluence: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PLAT/pages/3456789/Fallthrough+Governance+notes
- Jira: PLAT-2028, PLAT-2071, INC-4392
- GitHub prototype: https://github.com/redwood/serving-controlplane/pull/904
- Internal dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/8g3/fallthrough-governor

Notes to reviewers:
- Keep defaults conservative; prioritize user-visible quality over marginal cost savings.
- Plan two drills next quarter (1 region outage, 1 model regression) to exercise the Governor end-to-end.
